sections.overview: Monopis obviella is a small tineid moth whose caterpillars recycle decaying organic material.
sections.identification: The adult’s wingspan is about 10–13 mm. Its wing pattern is easily confused with that of the close relative Monopis crocicapitella, and the two were historically confused.
sections.habitat: Adults are recorded in Britain mainly in southern England and may be found around buildings as well as outdoors.
sections.diet: The caterpillars scavenge animal and plant refuse, including woollen material and detritus in bird nests or raptor pellets.
sections.behavior: Adults fly mainly from May to October and are sometimes attracted to lights.
sections.reproduction: Two generations are considered likely in Britain, though this is not firmly established.
sections.ecology: Its larvae are scavengers rather than plant-feeding pests; confusion with Monopis crocicapitella has made the species’ distribution harder to map.
sections.conservation: It is recorded locally in Britain, but historical misidentifications make regional distribution estimates uncertain.
